messages.body_plain:
Jim,

> I was suprised to read, "As administrators, our most troubling issue
> was a mentor proposal that received almost unanimous criticism from
> other mentors as scientiﬁcally unsound"

Well, I'm surprised that you are surprised.

> Would you please remind us of the numeric scores and their context for
> the proposal in question?

IMHO that is exactly the problem: the scoring can evaluate the quality
of the _student's_ proposal
They can help to sort things, but the quality of the student proposal
alone is not sufficient for a successful project. Which is why we
started to discuss other boundary conditions.

However, I'll try to clarify the text.

> It seems to me that you are using the words "almost unanimous" in a
> sense in which they are very rarely used.

As I'm not a native English speaker that may be the case - though I
think John knows English langugage. I took is as a _polite_ description
of what happened.

If you prefer "n - 1", we could change the text. If I did miss someone
besides you who did express the opinion that the project was
statistically sound, please come forward so we can write n - 2 etc.

Best,

Claudia

messages.subject: Google Code-In Mailing List
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Dianne cook has set up a mailing list to discuss Google Code-In issues.
You can join the list from this web page:

http://groups.google.com/group/gci-r?hl=en

A wikipage has also been set up to collect ideas for tasks:

http://rwiki.sciviews.org/doku.php?id=developers:projects:gci2011&s=google%20code

If you are interested in participating in Google Code-In, please, join
the mailing list to discuss your ideas and keep the wiki updated. We are
still waiting to know whether the R Foundation will be accepted as a
participating institution but the list tasks will be taken into account
when considering our application.

Google Code-in is a Google's contest to introduce pre-university
students (age 13-18) to the many kinds of contributions that make open
source software development possible.

Best regards,

--
Virgilio Gómez-Rubio
Departamento de Matemáticas
Escuela de Ingenieros Industriales
Universidad de Castilla-La Mancha
Avda España s/n
02071 Albacete - SPAIN

already has) are more statistically sound that stepwise regression
techniques which can model growth curves?  I have several authorities

messages.subject: Re: paper about GSoC 2011
messages.body_plain:
GSoC11 is now finished, but it appears that there is still ongoing
discussion about a project that the majority of mentors felt was
scientifically unsound.
This is NOT a message to further one side or the other of that issue,
but to point out that Google is funding code, not scientific investigations.

It is the main job of "project" (i.e., R GSoC) admins to administer, not
to make the scientific decisions. I would not, as admin, oppose a
project where I held the minority view. Whether the majority is right or
wrong will be revealed by future developments. Much of my own work was
ignored by the computational community for many years as it was not
mainstream -- now optim() seems to get more use than even I would like.
However, in trying to play referee and bring decision-making to a
conclusion on a very tight deadline, Claudia Beleites and I received
some criticisms and commentary we felt were abusive.

I propose that any further discussion of the merit or not of project
ideas for an activity that is now historical should cease on this list,
with the sanction being that the list will be appropriately edited
otherwise.

Time for GSoC12.

John Nash

--

messages.subject: Re: becoming a mentor
messages.body_plain:
Essentially you indicate your willingness and suitability for a particular project idea.
We really want to have a couple of mentors per student who is funded. You may also suggest
some ideas. Remember these are CODING projects, not research ones, but work towards a
research project or thesis is allowed, so packaging some tools would be a possibility, but
the ideas themselves should already be expressed somewhere.

Have a look back at the list of suggested projects. On the R-wiki are some pages related
to earlier years as well.

Note that things are a bit of a lottery. Sometimes a great idea gets a weak student
(because the students must take the ideas and prepare a work-plan). Students can also
propose ideas, in which case they'll be looking for a mentor. Then we have to score the
student plans and match to the number of slots Google gives us. Last year it was 15. And
then one good student got a job, but in time to be replaced, but another lost his way and
we failed him at the mid-term. Life's like that. We also had a good student who was going
to work on a project that most of the mentor group felt was scientifically unsound. The
admins felt very much like the peanut butter in a sandwich held by a very strong 3-year
old as we tried to deal with that.

Despite all these issues, GSoC has some benefits beyond the direct ones. For example, it
does get some ideas out in the open, and it allows a number of R user/developers to
interact to try to advance the whole. It also earns a little bit of money for R -- $7500
this year at $500 per student mentored. Two mentors also get travel money to the Mentors'
summit at Google in October, and get to meet and interact with other software developers.

Best, JN
